findings.problem: decision_logic[2] covers a prescription on which 'the only sign of the practitioner's wishes is the signature, a pre-selected default or some element other than a unique "no substitution" indication' and directs the pharmacist to 'proceed as on a prescription on which "no substitution" has not been indicated', that is, to fill it and interchange. For the pre-selected default that action is wrong. A prescription whose 'no substitution' indication is the default does not meet 105 CMR 721.020(B)(1), and under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform to 105 CMR 721.000 is invalid and shall not be filled. The same applies to a form that lacks the required interchange statement (721.020(B)(2)) or makes the signature the 'no substitution' mechanism (721.020(B)(3)). The section never mentions 721.040(A). orientation[1], common_traps[0] and forms_records[0] correctly say a default or a signature is not the indication, but they give no consequence, which leaves decision_logic[2] as the section's only answer.
findings.rationale: 721.020 is headed 'Prescription Formats'. Paragraph (B) sets format conditions, 721.020(F) applies them to written prescriptions, and 721.003 applies the standards to every prescription issued by a practitioner or reduced to writing by a pharmacist. 721.040(A) says a nonconforming format 'is invalid and shall not be filled'. The section is right that a signature on a conforming prescription does not supply 'no substitution', and in that case interchange is mandated. But a candidate given a pre-checked or defaulted 'no substitution' would, following the section, dispense an interchange on a prescription the regulation says may not be filled at all. The repair is at sentence level: confine the 'proceed' action to a conforming prescription that carries no unique indication, and state that a format which makes 'no substitution' the default, omits the interchange statement or lets the signature serve as the indication is invalid under 721.040(A), so the pharmacist does not fill it until a conforming prescription is obtained.

findings.problem: The section says interchangeability in Massachusetts 'is therefore a question of listing'. Its method for deciding the question is the appendix lookup and nothing else: an Orange Book 'A'-rated product not on the Exception List, or otherwise a product on the Additional List, minus the 105 CMR 720.060 exclusions. It leaves out the Department's own rule for products made under the same NDA as the brand. The introduction in the 105 CMR 720.200 appendix says generic products manufactured under the same NDA as the brand are therapeutically equivalent, that Massachusetts regulations allow their interchange, and that their distributors and repackagers are not identified in the Orange Book. DCP Circular Letter 22-01-112 (January 14, 2022) says an authorized generic is not specifically listed in the Orange Book but is considered therapeutically equivalent to its brand, so a pharmacist may interchange it for a brand-name prescription unless the prescriber indicated 'no substitution'. Following the section's lookup, a candidate would find an authorized generic neither in the Orange Book nor on the Additional List and would conclude that it cannot be interchanged.
findings.rationale: Learning objective 3 declares this scope: 'Decide whether a product is interchangeable in Massachusetts' by working through the MLID. The omitted rule appears in 105 CMR 720.000's own appendix and is repeated in a current Drug Control Program circular letter, and authorized generics are common in dispensing. The omission therefore gives a wrong answer on an ordinary Massachusetts fact pattern, not only a remote one. The repair: add the same-NDA and authorized-generic path, which is still subject to a 'no substitution' indication, to orientation[3] and decision_logic[6], and qualify 'a question of listing' in orientation[3] and in comparison_tables[0].rows[2].

findings.problem: Department texts that the section relies on, or sends candidates to, still disagree with the current M.G.L. c. 112, s. 12D, and the section does not warn of it. 105 CMR 720.010 says a pharmacist must interchange 'when a prescription written by a practitioner indicates "interchange"'. The Foreword in the 105 CMR 720.200 appendix says a prescriber who wants the brand must sign and write 'no substitution' in his or her own handwriting below the signature line, and it describes a nine-member commission, whereas c. 17, s. 13(a) now provides for 16 members. Part II of the DCP policy and the DCP MLID page both state the duty as dispensing the less expensive interchangeable product, without the statute's first direction to an interchangeable abuse deterrent product.
findings.rationale: The section teaches the current s. 12D and 105 CMR 721.020(B) correctly and repeats none of these older statements, so this alone does not mislead. It is Low and would not by itself prevent a KEEP. Still, a candidate who opens 105 CMR 720.000 or the policy, as the section invites, will meet contrary text. One sentence saying that s. 12D as amended controls over the older Department descriptions would prevent that confusion.

results.summary: I checked the whole section against current official text and found it accurate on almost every point. That covers: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 12D (the format mandate, the signature, the 'no substitution' standards, the abuse-deterrent-first order and its c. 17, s. 13(b) opiate formulary, the label form, the complaint route, the hospital exemption and its provisos, and the MassHealth notice for narrow therapeutic index transplant immunosuppressants, which goes to the prescribing physician and sets no time or method); 105 CMR 721.020(B); 105 CMR 720.050-720.090 and the appendix lookup, Exception List and Additional List; 247 CMR 9.05(1)-(3)(e), including both emergency limbs, the date/hour/nature record, the purchaser's written acceptance, Board review and the Drug Store reach; 247 CMR 9.19(1)(a) and (24); the DCP midstream policy, correctly labelled as guidance with its 'should' flagged; s. 12EE(a)-(g), covering both FDA routes, the written patient-specific bar, the prescriber notice and its method order, the written patient notice and the one-year record measured from the last profile entry; and c. 94C, s. 21C(a)-(d) with c. 176O, s. 1, including the PBM-contract clause. All five practice questions (MA-Q-0087, 0113, 0226, 0391, 0433) can be answered from the section and none is contradicted. Two Medium defects need sentence-level repair. (1) decision_logic[2] tells the pharmacist to fill and interchange a prescription whose only 'no substitution' sign is a pre-selected default. Such a format fails 105 CMR 721.020(B)(1) and is invalid and shall not be filled under 105 CMR 721.040(A), which the section never mentions. (2) The interchangeability lookup ('a question of listing') leaves out the Department's same-NDA/authorized-generic rule (the introduction in the 105 CMR 720.200 appendix and DCP Circular Letter 22-01-112), so a candidate would wrongly treat an authorized generic as not interchangeable. One Low note: the section could warn that 105 CMR 720.010, the 720.200 Foreword, the DCP policy and the MLID page still describe the superseded handwritten/'indicates interchange' format or leave out the abuse deterrent step. The failed criteria (decision_logic, material_exceptions, study_usefulness_without_legal_distortion) all come from the two Medium findings. Disposition: MINOR_EDIT.
